title: How to Repair Relationships (And Why You Might As Well Accept that You’ll Need To) need-to/
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that teacher-student relationships decay by default, borrowing the second law of thermodynamics as a metaphor for entropy in the social realm. Having said elsewhere that relationships are not the point of school, he still holds that caring relationships bolster a teacher's credibility and make the work richer. His move is to elevate relationship repair above relationship building as the skill teachers neglect, since a teacher manages dozens or hundreds of relationships and some will inevitably break. He walks through a case of a student, Mariah, whose bad mood the teacher misreads and jokes about, causing offense. The prescription is simple: acknowledge that intent does not erase offense, privately ask the student whether you hurt her, and apologize if so. He admits this offers no control over the student's forgiveness, but it is within the teacher's control every day, and he closes by telling teachers to drop self-flagellation and keep moving.
points: Relationships with students tend toward disrepair, so teachers should expect and plan for repair rather than treat breakdowns as failures.
Repair matters because offense is real to the student even when the teacher did not intend it and an impartial observer would call it harmless.
The mechanism is a private, quick check-in: ask whether you offended the student and apologize if the answer is yes.
If the student says no, use the moment to say her feelings matter and invite her to tell you if it happens, which opens the channel for later.
Teachers should not berate themselves after offending someone; do the repair, extract the lesson, and move on.
quotes: I’ve written a lot about how relationships aren’t the point of school — it’s actually not “all about relationships” — but they sure are important. Perhaps most critically, caring relationships enhance my credibility; they also make teaching a lot richer and more fun.

But building relationships is only the first skill you need to practice; relationship repair is a critical skill, too. Why? Because if you are a school teacher, you’ve got dozens or hundreds of individual relationships going on this school year. You might as well expect some of them to need fixing at some point.
The second law of thermodynamics seems to exist not just in the natural universe, but in the social realm, too. Relationships tend toward disrepair.
And there you go! I’ve done the worst thing I can possibly do for my credibility: I’ve offended her.

It’s not a silver bullet process; it doesn’t give me omnipotent control over the heart of Mariah. I can’t require her to forgive me — heck, I can’t even require her to tell me that I’ve done something hurtful.
But I can pull her aside and I can genuinely seek to make amends. That is in my control, every day.
